US first lady Melania Trump will host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, the Trump administration has said.
Her office said that she would personally bring unnamed officials from the warring countries together in an “extraordinary moment in American history”.
“This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American first lady,” the White House said, adding that she would also deliver remarks about the ceasefire in the Ukrainian town of Oleshky, which she was involved in brokering.
The announcement came amid a major attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and following a devastating Russian strike on a school being used for aid distribution in Zaporizhzhia that killed at least 33 people.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko described the situation with power in the capital as “extremely difficult” and said the attacks “create a threat not only to Ukraine but also to nuclear safety throughout Europe.”
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles overnight, hitting power plants and substations from the Black Sea port of Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west.

Russian forces conducted a large, combined drone and missile strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight on November 2 to 3 as part of Russia’s strike campaign aimed at inflicting increasing costs on Ukrainian society and coercing Ukraine into capitulating over the winter.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike against Ukraine overnight, primarily targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in nine oblasts and causing widespread power outages.
[1] Zelensky stated that Russian forces launched 289 strike drones, 17 ballistic missiles, and 59 cruise missiles, and data from the Ukrainian Air Force suggests that Ukrainian forces intercepted only 17.
65 percent of ballistic and anti-ship missiles while intercepting 83.
05 percent of cruise missiles.
[2] The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that Russian forces struck four power plants and two electrical substations across Ukraine, and a Kremlin-affiliated milblogger claimed that Russian forces struck at least six power plants.
[3] Ukrainian state energy operator Ukrenergo reported that Russian forces targeted Ukraine’s energy facilities more than 20 times overnight and during the day on November 3, inflicting serious damage and launching one of the largest strikes on energy infrastructure since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
Ukrenergo added that strikes caused power outages in at least five oblasts.
[4] These strikes coincide with the beginning of the residential heating season across Ukraine, including in Kyiv City, which Kyiv City Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko announced started on November 2.
[5]
Polish authorities prevented a Russian provocation along Poland’s international border with Russia on the night of November 2 to 3. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reported on November 3 that Polish authorities mobilized resources to prevent a provocation near Sepopol, Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship, Poland, after Polish border guards observed individuals carrying flashlights along Poland’s international border with Kaliningrad Oblast, Russia.[6] Tusk added that the “tension and escalation from Russia” may continue and that Poland should be ready to prevent any possible future provocations. Polish authorities have also taken steps to strengthen security along the Polish-Russian border following recent intelligence warnings and an increase in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.[7]
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov likely indirectly responded to Poland’s recent defensive measures against Russia by falsely framing Poland as the aggressor. Lavrov claimed on November 3 that Poland and the Baltic States are the “most active promoters” of Europe’s “reactionary and aggressive” policies towards Russia.[8] Kremlin officials regularly and baselessly attempt to frame European measures to strengthen its defense posture as evidence of aggression against Russia, despite Russia’s increased kinetic and cyber activity within Europe.[9] Lavrov is likely attempting to cast Poland as the aggressor against Russia to simultaneously obfuscate the real Russian threat to Europe and sow domestic division within Poland.
Ukrainian, US, and Russian officials provided new details on upcoming trilateral negotiations set to take place on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff stated on November 2 that the United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia, and that discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, and humanitarian efforts.[10] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on November 3 that the trilateral negotiations will be in a team-level format to pave the way for future leader-level negotiations.[11] Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov announced on November 3 that Russian Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky will head the Russian delegation during the trilateral negotiations.[12] Medinsky led the previous Russian delegation to trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, in February 2026 and used his position to stall negotiations by discussing the so-called “historical roots” of the war — terminology which Ukrainian and US officials have previously noted that Kremlin officials bring up during negotiations to distract from discussions of a serious peace deal.[13] Medinsky’s role as lead negotiator indicates that the Kremlin remains disinterested in engaging in good-faith negotiations and is instead committed to a protracted war effort against Ukraine.[14]
The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) and regional authorities are increasingly cutting and delaying non-essential military and recruitment expenditures amid failures to adequately address rising budget deficits.
Russian opposition source Verstka reported on October 30 that the Russian MoD proposed a draft order to postpone December payments for Russian military personnel not fighting in Ukraine to January 2027.
[15] St.
Petersburg online newspaper Fontanka reported on November 3, citing responses from the St.
Petersburg military enlistment office, that St.
Petersburg reduced its regional one-time recruitment bonuses to 400,000 rubles (roughly $4,940), down from one million rubles (roughly $12,350) in mid-October 2026 and 3.
5 million rubles (roughly $43,224) before October 2026.
[16] These bonuses do not include federal payments of 400,000 rubles from the Russian MoD.
A Russian propagandist claimed on November 3 that Russian regional authorities have also widely reduced or eliminated death benefits for families of deceased servicemembers throughout 2026, citing compensation cuts ranging from 50 to 100 percent of the original payments in at least a dozen federal subjects.
[17] Russia’s force generation model relies on increasingly expensive financial incentives to maintain recruitment rates and avoid a politically risky general mobilization as inflation and battlefield casualties continue to increase.
[18] The Kremlin and Russian federal subjects have reduced social spending to finance Russian offensive capabilities and expanded taxes and exports to generate new revenue.
The Kremlin is now likely seeking further fiscal relief by cutting military expenditures outside the Ukraine war effort.
[19]
The Kremlin is weaponizing limited information about an internal Ukrainian clash to exploit genuine concern over mobilization and stoke division in Ukrainian society.
Ukraine’s security officials confirmed on November 3 that a clash broke out between protesters and National Guard servicemembers outside a building in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka, Kyiv Oblast, on November 2, after unknown actors disseminated unconfirmed video appeals accusing Ukrainian servicemembers illegally detaining people nearby.
[20] Ukraine’s National Guard confirmed that it officially rented the facility as a temporary accommodation point for mobilized personnel and that there were four people receiving medical assistance at the location after their detention for going absent without leave (AWOL).
[21] The Kyiv Oblast Police stated that Ukrainian military personnel were staying in the building and refuted claims about the alleged detention of any citizens.
[22] Ukrainian Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov stated on November 3 that Ukrainian law enforcement is investigating the details of the incident and acknowledged that the incident demonstrated genuine tension in Ukraine about mobilization policies that Ukraine needs to resolve.
[23] Budanov implied that the clashes may have involved “provocateurs,” and Ukrainian authorities detained a woman posing as a medic at the site.
[24] Budanov stated that the woman had purchased an ambulance and inspected the site prior to the incident, and had corresponded with Telegram channels that were spreading information about the incident.
[25]
Russian officials and state media have weaponized the incident to stoke and amplify existing tensions within Ukrainian society regarding mobilization. Senior Kremlin officials described the house as a “torture chamber” and Russian milbloggers spread unconfirmed accusations that the Ukrainian forces tortured, extorted, forcibly mobilized, and murdered people in the building’s basement.[26] Moscow is likely exploiting the lack of confirmed information about the incident to spread inflammatory and unsubstantiated claims in an effort to sow discord in Ukrainian society.

- Polish authorities prevented a Russian provocation along Poland’s international border with Russia on the night of November 2 to 3.
- Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov likely indirectly responded to Poland’s recent defensive measures against Russia by falsely framing Poland as the aggressor.

- Ukrainian forces continued their long-range strike campaign against Russian oil infrastructure in Yaroslavl Oblast.

articles.full_text:
November 4, 2026 | 06:20 am
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had seen no sign that Russia is serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy and Merz both said the European Union must help shape any lasting peace.
Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.
"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."
Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.
"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.
Europe must have a say on postwar security
Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.
He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.
The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.
"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.
He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.
Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians
The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.
Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.
Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.
Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."
On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.
Germany pledges aid ahead of winter
"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.
Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.
"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.
He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.
How has Berlin stepped up security?
The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.
Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war: Strikes on a school by Russia kills 26, derailing hopes of progress toward peace - The Hindu
articles.summary: Russia-Ukraine war: Strikes on a school by Russia kills 26, derailing hopes of progress toward peace  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
Ukraine said Monday (November 2, 2026) that Russian strikes on a school distributing humanitarian aid killed at least 26 people, dashing fragile hopes of "progress toward peace" after a local ceasefire in the south expired without violations.
Russia resumed its strikes on the southern region of Kherson after the end of a ceasefire in the area, the longest truce in the war raging between the neighbours since Russia's 2022 invasion, Kyiv said.
A rare pause in the fighting, brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to enable a mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, ended Sunday (November 1, 2026) after starting on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), with neither side reporting breaches.
But hours after the truce, Russia targeted a village in Zaporizhzhia, adjacent to Kherson, with repeated strikes that killed at least 26 people, the acting regional Governor said.
Some of the dead had come to collect aid at a local school.
Footage posted by the Ukrainian emergency services showed the building reduced to piles of smouldering rubble and rescuers working at the site.
"Every Monday, humanitarian aid was distributed to people there," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his daily address.
"The Russians carried out the first strike just as people arrived. Then, there was a repeat strike, more aerial bombs, this time targeting the shelter."
Among those killed were "two rescue workers and four police officers", acting regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram.
The service named the rescuers as two 44-year-olds: Denys Konovalenko and Oleksy Sushchevsky.
"Every day, they went out to help people, working in dangerous conditions and risking their own lives to save others," it said in a statement.
Mr. Zelensky said that after the Oleshky truce, "there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible".
"With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings. There must be a response to this."
Russia fortifies positions
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, which is grinding through its fifth year after killing hundreds of thousands of people and displacing millions.
A senior Ukrainian figure told AFP on Sunday (November 1, 2026) that Russia refused a Ukrainian offer to extend the truce.
Kyiv's military also alleged that Moscow had used the pause in fighting to "fortify its positions".
The Kremlin did not deny the accusations, with its spokesperson Dmitry Peskov telling reporters Monday (November 2, 2026): "This is a completely normal practice in such situations."
He alleged the Ukrainian Army had also used pauses in fighting in the past to regroup.
Moscow saw the Oleshky humanitarian mission as "successful", Mr. Peskov added, praising the "good cooperation between all sides" and singling out the role of its human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova.
Ms. Lantratova oversaw the ceasefire alongside her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets in one of the most substantial instances of Russian-Ukrainian cooperation since the start of the war.
The mission saw people evacuated to both Ukraine-controlled territory and Moscow-annexed Crimea.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned "at the moment".
U.S.-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next week, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday (November 2, 2026).
President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the dragging war but there has been no breakthrough.
The talks, to be held November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi, Mr. Witkoff said, come as Kyiv and its European allies worry that Mr. Trump has increasingly sided with Moscow.
Cyberattacks
Both Russia and Ukraine said overnight that their emergency warnings apps were hacked in apparent cyberattacks that came hours after the truce had ended.
Ukraine said it suspected its air raid alert system had been compromised, after false alerts of a radiation threat were sent to millions.
The warning system provides vital information about incoming Russian drones and missiles.
Russia has intensified its attacks this year, firing ballistic missiles and fast jet-powered drones, both of which are hard to intercept.
Moscow said that an app belonging to its emergency situations ministry that also warns of attacks had been hacked, too.
The app is not widely used in Russia, where warnings of Ukrainian drone attacks are not as common and typically sent by text message in border regions.

articles.summary: Middle Corridor Traffic Surges as Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan Deepen Trade Integration  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Representatives from Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are accelerating efforts to formalize and expand the Middle Corridor, a rapidly growing multimodal trade route that bypasses Russia to link Asian manufacturing hubs with European markets. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route has emerged as a critical geopolitical and economic artery, with container traffic surging by 450 percent over recent periods as global supply chains adapt to ongoing sanctions against Moscow.
Spanning Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey, the corridor offers a vital alternative to the traditional Northern rail routes that have been severely disrupted by the war in Ukraine and subsequent Western sanctions. As China and Central Asian republics seek reliable export pathways, the Middle Corridor has transitioned from a niche logistical option to a cornerstone of Eurasian trade strategy.
Institutional Integration and Foreign Investment
The push for deeper integration is anchored by significant institutional milestones. In 2023, railway operators from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Georgia established the Middle Corridor Multimodal consortium to streamline customs procedures and coordinate freight schedules across borders. The initiative gained substantial momentum in August 2025 when China formally joined the joint venture, signaling Beijing's commitment to diversifying its Belt and Road logistics away from Russian territory.
According to the World Bank, sustained investment in the corridor's infrastructure could triple regional trade volumes, reduce transit times by nearly half, and boost the collective GDP of participating nations by 3.3 percent. The financial institution estimates that the development of the route could create up to two million jobs across nine Eurasian countries by 2040, provided that participating governments implement synchronized digital customs systems and upgrade port facilities.
Overcoming Caspian Bottlenecks
Despite the route's strategic promise, logistical bottlenecks continue to constrain its maximum capacity. The Caspian Sea remains the principal chokepoint, requiring cargo to be transferred from rail networks onto ferries before being reloaded onto trains in Azerbaijan. This multimodal transfer adds days to transit times and increases costs, particularly during adverse weather conditions.
Compounding the maritime challenge is the long-term environmental issue of the shrinking Caspian Sea, which threatens the draft capacity of ports and the viability of heavy ferry operations. To address these physical constraints, regional powers are pouring capital into infrastructure. Turkey recently announced a $10 billion investment plan aimed at eliminating rail bottlenecks along its eastern borders, intending to create a seamless, high-capacity freight line that connects directly to the European network via the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway.
China's Role and the Digital Silk Road
China's entry into the consortium has fundamentally altered the corridor's economic calculus. Beijing is not merely a transit client but an active investor, having committed billions toward modernizing Kazakhstan's rail links and upgrading the port of Aktau. This integration aligns with China's broader strategy to secure overland export routes that are immune to maritime blockades or naval disruptions in the Strait of Malacca.
Furthermore, the push for a digital customs framework along the corridor is gaining traction. Stakeholders are developing unified blockchain-based platforms designed to allow cargo to clear inspections digitally before it even reaches a border crossing. This digital integration is viewed as essential to reducing the dwell times that currently plague the Caspian crossings, potentially shaving up to a week off the total transit time from western China to the European Union.
Geopolitical Significance and Market Resilience
For global markets, the maturation of the Middle Corridor represents a structural shift in supply chain resilience. Western logistics firms and multinational manufacturers have increasingly routed cargo through the Caspian to avoid the legal and reputational risks associated with Russian transit. This shift has spurred private investment in warehousing and dry ports in cities like Aktau in Kazakhstan and Alat in Azerbaijan.
However, the route's expansion requires delicate diplomatic balancing. The participating nations must maintain functional trade relations with both Western economies and their traditional partners in the Eurasian Economic Union. As Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan deepen their cooperation, the focus is shifting toward standardizing tariffs, investing in automated tracking systems, and expanding the physical footprint of Caspian ports to handle the projected volume of containerized goods over the next decade.
As global supply chains continue to fracture along geopolitical lines, the Middle Corridor stands as a testament to the market's ability to forge new pathways when traditional arteries are blocked, ensuring that Eurasian commerce remains resilient in an era of unprecedented strategic competition.

articles.title: COMMENT: Azerbaijan's arrival turns Central Asia's C5 into a Caspian C6 - CACI - IntelliNews
articles.summary: COMMENT: Azerbaijan's arrival turns Central Asia's C5 into a Caspian C6 - CACI  IntelliNews
articles.full_text:
Azerbaijan's entry into Central Asia's leaders' club puts the Caspian at the centre of a six-country push for joint production, CACI Analyst argued in an analysis on November 2.
The eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia, held in Awaza on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast on October 8, was the first at which Azerbaijan sat as a full member. The leaders signed a joint statement, adopted the format's regulatory documents and handed Baku the chair for 2027, according to the paper by Yunis Gurbanov, a senior adviser at the AIR Center think tank in Baku, published by the Washington-based Central Asia-Caucasus Institute.
The enlargement shifts the format's geography and its agenda without turning it into a supra-national body or an integration bloc. The forum still runs on consensus and keeps its flexibility deliberately, but with Baku inside, Trans-Caspian transport, energy and the ecology of the sea now sit at the top of the agenda. Baku's arrival creates a new regional concept built around connectivity while leaving the group's identity intact, according to Gurbanov.
From guest to member
The consultative format grew out of the thaw in regional relations that followed the change of leadership in Uzbekistan in 2016. Rather than build another treaty-based intergovernmental organisation, the five former Soviet republics set up a leaders' mechanism for consultation and coordination. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev restated that preference in Awaza, speaking out against "cumbersome structures" and in favour of a flexible format of sovereign states.
Azerbaijan attended earlier meetings as a guest as its political, economic and transport ties with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan deepened. The Central Asian presidents accepted it as a full participant in Tashkent in November 2025, and an informal meeting at Lake Issyk-Kul that ended with the Cholpon-Ata Declaration on July 31 prepared the ground for the first formal six-way summit.
Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev told the Awaza meeting that his country's trade with Central Asia had grown by 50% over the past year and that more than 400 companies with Central Asian capital operate in Azerbaijan. Baku has set up joint investment funds with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.
Six economies, one product
The most important idea to come out of Awaza was Mirziyoyev's "six economies - one product" formula, under which companies across the six countries would work in shared value chains instead of simply selling to one another, according to Gurbanov. Uzbekistan also proposed a Central Asia-Azerbaijan business forum in Khiva in 2027.
Aliyev made a matching pitch to the summit. "We should not limit ourselves to increasing mutual trade, but also invest, produce and enter foreign markets together," he said. Pursued in earnest, that means more industrial zones, factories, logistics centres and investment projects along the corridor, according to Gurbanov.
Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put a number on the ambition, proposing to lift trade among the six from about $13bn in 2025 to at least $20bn. He also conceded that only a small share of the more than 200 initiatives tabled in the C5 format since 2018 had been carried out.
The leaders adopted rules for the meeting and Uzbekistan proposed a dedicated legal framework, but Mirziyoyev told the summit that implementation mattered more than the number of documents signed. More institutions could improve coordination, while too much formality risks killing the flexibility that has kept the format alive, according to Gurbanov.
The sea in the middle
Transport is likely to remain the most practical area of cooperation, according to Gurbanov. The Middle Corridor runs through Azerbaijan to link Central Asia with Georgia, Turkey and Europe, and has grown in importance for Central Asian states looking for routes to western markets across the Caspian. Cargo on the route rose by more than 10% in 2025 and by nearly 20% in the first eight months of 2026, Aliyev said. Uzbekistan proposed a Council for Infrastructure Development to coordinate transport projects and tie national networks into a regional system, a plan that dovetails with the expansion of the Baku International Sea Trade Port.
Kazakh and Turkmen oil already moves through Azerbaijan's transport network, the grid operators of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are developing a green energy corridor to export power westwards, and Baku and Astana have begun laying a subsea fibre-optic cable across the Caspian.
Azerbaijan has raised the alarm over the falling level of the Caspian, which threatens coastal infrastructure and would make shipping across it costlier and less efficient.
Turkic overlap, Russian ties
Baku's membership also brings the C6 closer to the Organisation of Turkic States (OTS), a mainstay of Azerbaijan's foreign policy. Four of the six are OTS members and Turkmenistan is an observer, while Tajikistan, with its distinct language and culture, works through other regional groupings. Aliyev proposed joint military exercises at the OTS summit in Gabala in October 2025 and returned to defence and security cooperation in September 2026, though Kazakhstan has rejected the idea of turning the Turkic group into a military alliance. The C6 is a broader platform that complements the OTS rather than competing with it, according to Gurbanov.
The six have different relationships with Russia, China, Turkey, the EU and the US. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan belong to the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are also members of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Turkmenistan clings to permanent neutrality and Tajikistan follows its own foreign and security priorities.
The C6 is neither a formal organisation nor an alliance, and its members keep their sovereignty and separate foreign policies. Its value lies in giving six states joined by the Caspian and increasingly bound together by transport, energy and investment corridors a place to line up their interests. Azerbaijan's first chairmanship in 2027 will be the test: if Baku can turn the Awaza proposals into concrete projects, the move from C5 to C6 could mark a real step towards cooperation across the whole Trans-Caspian region, according to Gurbanov.

articles.title: China turns to intl media to promote gains of Belt and Road Initiative - The Manila Times

FUZHOU, China — China called on international media to report on the gains and benefits of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) program to participating countries.
At the opening of the 2026 Media Cooperation Forum on Belt and Road here on Tuesday, Chinese officials and business leaders cited the need for global action in what they called “the world’s largest international platform for economic cooperation in terms of scale, reach and impact.”
Xian Hui, vice chairman of the National Communist of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPC), said the BRI, which President Xi Jinping started in 2013, was no longer just focused on development and investment initiatives originally intended to link East Asia and Europe through physical infrastructure.
He said it has evolved into “modernist socialization,” which called for a “deeper alignment of development strategies, improving connectivity networks and balancing development with security by providing an environment that would bring peace, prosperity, openness and civilization.” Hu Heping, the executive deputy head of publicity for the department of the CPC Central Committee, said that amid the “rise of conflicts, unilateralism and challenges of copyright infringements,” there was a need to “build a consensus for development, tell stories that benefit people and deepen exchanges of cooperation by building bridges of communication.”
Zhang Tao, president of the China National Nuclear Corp.; Wang Jihang, president of the Agricultural Bank of China; Oleg Kopylov, deputy secretary general, Shanghai Cooperation Organization; Miao Jiianmin, chairman, China Merchants Group; Zhao Fei, board member and general manager, China Changan Automobile Group; Xu Siwei, chairman, China Reform Holdings Corp.; and Zhang Wenwu, vice chairman and president, CITIC Group Corp., were among the business leaders who pushed for greater “connectivity” through the media to help boost international cooperation by sharing “people-to-people experiences, cultural and financial integration.”
The event brought together over 200 foreign representatives from 100 countries, as well as international and regional organizations, and 182 media outlets and institutions, People’s Daily, China’s English-language newspaper, said.
BRI, sometimes referred to as the New Silk Road, is considered “one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects ever conceived.”
To date, about 150 countries were known to have signed memoranda of understanding with China.
The Philippines became a member of the BRI in 2018 under then-president Rodrigo Duterte, linking Chinese foreign investments to the administration’s “Build, Build, Build” program.
The initiative involved proposed and active transport, water and energy projects — such as the Binondo-Intramuros Bridge, the Chico River Pump Irrigation Project, and the New Centennial Water Source (Kaliwa Dam).
Under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., however, enthusiasm for the BRI waned over tensions in the South China Sea.

articles.title: How China Is Building Influence in Central Asia, One Laboratory at a Time - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: How China Is Building Influence in Central Asia, One Laboratory at a Time  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
For years, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has been presented as a set of trade routes. While infrastructure projects are crucial for growth, another part of China’s work in Central Asia gets much less attention: the links between universities and laboratories.
Uzbekistan is a good example. In October 2026, the second meeting of the Uzbekistan-China Expert Council convened in Tashkent to discuss “Digital Partnership: Artificial Intelligence and the Next-Generation Data Economy.” The meeting demonstrates that China’s engagement with Central Asia does not neglect knowledge networks and scientific cooperation. This matters because scientific partnerships often outlast commercial projects and can shape who trains future researchers and provides access to advanced technologies. Indeed, such meetings start a recurring mechanism through which Chinese and Uzbek academics and technology specialists formulate ideas, standards, and research priorities together.
According to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, trade with China reached $13.07 billion in 2024. Uzbekistan exported goods worth $2.64 billion and imported goods worth $10.43 billion. Yet trade figures alone reveal only part of the relationship. Increasingly, Beijing and Tashkent are investing in knowledge production. In September 2025, the two governments signed a cooperation program that links the “Uzbekistan–2030” strategy with the BRI. They also signed agreements on training people and on the digital economy.
In November 2025, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Higher Education, Science, and Innovation reported that universities in the two countries had launched 29 joint study programs in 2024-2025. Another development was the creation of the Muhammad al-Khwarizmi International Mathematical Center at Urgench State University, in partnership with Peking University.
Universities can train talent but their impact ultimately depends on the infrastructure available to convert research into practical outcomes. This is where laboratories are becoming increasingly important. In May 2025, Uzbekistan’s national news agency reported an agreement with a Chinese agricultural technology company to set up a food safety laboratory center. It also reported talks on a laboratory with the Tashkent Institute of Chemical Technology and Xi’an Petroleum University.
We should read such news with care. An agreement or a plan is not the same as a working laboratory that produces research. Still, these reports show where institutions plan to spend their time and money.
By 2026, laboratory initiatives had become part of a broader institutional effort to define priority areas. At the seventh meeting of the Uzbekistan-China subcommission on science and technology cooperation, officials agreed to expand joint projects in artificial intelligence (AI), digital technologies, agricultural biotechnology, new materials, and green energy. They also agreed to work on research facilities, systems that help turn research into business, joint funds, technology parks, and exchanges for young researchers. The key question now is how many of these plans will become real programs with clear results.
Building scientific capacity also requires systems that can protect and commercialize new ideas. Intellectual property (IP) is therefore another important part of the picture. In July 2026, during the meetings of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) in Geneva, China’s National Intellectual Property Administration signed two documents with Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Justice. The first is a memorandum on IP cooperation. The second is a Patent Prosecution Highway agreement, which helps patent offices in both countries review applications faster. These agreements open the door to closer patent cooperation. But on their own, they do not show that the two countries now file more joint patents or sell more joint technologies. The official sources used for this article do not give regular data on joint patents, licensed technologies, or research results that have reached the market.
The same shift from traditional cooperation to knowledge-based cooperation is visible in emerging technologies. In July 2026, Uzbekistan became a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. This should not be seen as only a China-Uzbekistan success, because the organization includes many countries. More directly, in October 2026, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies met China’s ambassador to discuss cooperation in AI, data security, and university training. On October 19, the second meeting of the Uzbekistan-China Expert Council in Tashkent discussed AI rules, digital infrastructure, technology transfer, investment, and skills.
Yet, as elsewhere in the partnership, discussions and agreements remain easier to identify than measurable outcomes. It is important to separate three things: an agreement, an activity that has started, and a measurable result. Announcing a new research center shows ambition. A joint degree program shows that work has begun. Patents, published papers, trained graduates, new technologies used by companies and income from licenses show real results. Without reliable and detailed data, it is too early to say that one country has pushed another out of Uzbekistan’s science system.
One of the most widely used indicators is scientific co-authorship. Chinese universities increasingly promote international co-authorship to expand research networks, raise global visibility, and strengthen their presence in leading scientific databases. When researchers in Uzbekistan collaborate with Chinese institutions, Chinese universities gain not only publications but also a stronger position in setting research agendas, defining priority fields and coordinating long-term research networks. Scientific leadership today is often built through repeated collaboration, access to funding, laboratory infrastructure, doctoral training and publication networks. Co-authorship therefore serves not only as a measure of cooperation but also as a mechanism for accumulating scientific influence over time.
The United States and European countries still play an important role in Uzbekistan’s universities and science ecosystem. A fair comparison would need the same kind of data for each partner: joint publications, citations, researcher exchanges, scholarships, jointly funded laboratories, patents, and links between universities and industry. This data should also be open to checking. It should state which database was used, how author affiliations were counted, which years were covered and when the data was collected. This article does not attempt such a comparison, but future studies should.
For Beijing, science cooperation is a way to stay engaged in the region over the long term. It is less visible than a railway, but it may last longer. For Washington, Brussels, and other partners, it is a reminder that their role in Central Asia should be judged not only by infrastructure loans or security talks, but also by the opportunities they offer young researchers and universities. These partnerships do not exclude each other. Uzbekistan can benefit from science cooperation with many countries at once.

DUSHANBE, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Closer cooperation between Tajikistan and China under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) will unlock greater potential for regional development, said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
"Tajikistan-China relations are taking on increasingly greater strategic significance," Maitdinova told Xinhua in a recent interview, citing China's growing economic cooperation with Central Asia and Tajikistan's efforts to diversify its economy.
The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1992, and elevated their ties to a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership in the new era in 2024, opening up new prospects for bilateral cooperation, said the expert.
Tajik President Emomali Rahmon's state visit to China in May 2026 set another milestone in bilateral relations, Maitdinova said. During the visit, the two sides signed a series of cooperation documents, including the Treaty on Permanent Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation, and the Joint Statement on Deepening the Comprehensive Strategic Cooperative Partnership in the New Era.
Maitdinova highlighted the importance of aligning Tajikistan's National Development Strategy for the period up to 2030 with the China-proposed BRI. Tajikistan, a landlocked country with mountainous terrain, is keen to develop transport corridors, while China can help strengthen cross-border economic connectivity, improve transport links and foster more resilient trade and production networks across Eurasia, she said.
Energy and water resources are another strategically important area in bilateral cooperation, Maitdinova noted. Tajikistan has considerable hydropower potential, but tapping it requires modernizing energy infrastructure, expanding grid capacity and securing long-term financing.
Chinese technology and investment can support the development of hydropower, renewable energy and digital management systems, she said.
Maitdinova also underscored the importance of bilateral cooperation on security, as both countries have a shared interest in closer coordination between law enforcement agencies to combat the "three evil forces" of terrorism, separatism and extremism.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. "As one of the organization's founding members, China has helped broaden its economic, technological and institutional agenda and strengthen cooperation on security," Maitdinova said.
The SCO and the BRI play different but complementary roles, she said. The SCO provides a political and institutional platform for coordinating the interests of member states, while the BRI promotes cooperation through infrastructure projects, investment and trade links. "Together, they create opportunities to develop cross-border transport corridors, energy networks, digital infrastructure and production chains," Maitdinova said.
"Overall, Tajikistan-China relations are characterized by a high level of political trust, expanding economic cooperation and a transition toward a more comprehensive model of strategic partnership," she said.■

Israel and Kazakhstan signed an agreement to prevent double taxation on Monday following more than a decade of negotiations, in a move aimed at facilitating bilateral investment and expanding economic cooperation.
The agreement was signed during the tenth meeting of the Israel-Kazakhstan Joint Economic Commission in Jerusalem, co-chaired by Ze'ev Elkin, representing the Finance Ministry, and Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The Foreign Ministry organized the meeting, which brought together representatives from 12 government ministries, including nine Kazakh deputy ministers. In addition to the taxation agreement, the two countries signed memoranda of understanding on artificial intelligence, labor, and cybersecurity, as well as a joint declaration on space cooperation and the commission's official protocol.
Israel, Kazakhstan expand economic cooperation in AI, energy, water technology
The agreements represent a further step in strengthening economic relations between Israel and Kazakhstan, Central Asia's largest economy, as both countries seek to expand cooperation in technology, infrastructure, and strategic industries.
Discussions at the commission focused on energy, water technologies, innovation, agriculture, investment, critical minerals, science, healthcare, and industrial standardization. The countries also identified shared challenges involving climate change, desertification, and water resource management, areas in which Israeli technological expertise could support Kazakhstan's development priorities.
The agreement on double taxation is expected to make cross-border business activity easier by establishing a framework for determining taxation rights and reducing the risk of the same income being taxed in both countries. However, the precise provisions and implementation date have not yet been publicly detailed.
Elkin welcomed the agreement, calling it a significant achievement after years of diplomatic and economic discussions.
"Relations between Israel and Kazakhstan have gained momentum over the past year, especially following the visits of the foreign minister and the president," he said. "The visit of the senior delegation led by Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister, Zhaslan Madiyev, is an important opportunity to expand cooperation between the two countries."
Elkin said the commission reflected a shared commitment to strengthening economic ties, noting the unusually large Kazakh delegation and the broad range of government agencies involved.
"We are working to advance cooperation in artificial intelligence and innovation, water, agriculture, and energy, which will contribute to the economies of both countries," he added. "I am especially pleased to sign the double taxation agreement, after more than a decade of negotiations, which will ease the burden on companies and investors and open new economic opportunities."
Kazakhstan deputy prime minister makes highest-level visit to Israel in decade
Madiyev, who also oversees Kazakhstan's national artificial intelligence development program, is the highest-ranking Kazakh official to visit Israel in the past ten years, the Foreign Ministry said.
He arrived at the head of an economic delegation comprising more than 50 senior government officials and representatives of state-owned companies, including deputy ministers and regional governors. The visit came approximately six months after President Isaac Herzog traveled to Kazakhstan in April 2026, and nine months after Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar visited Astana in January.
During his visit, Madiyev met with Herzog, Sa'ar, Foreign Ministry Director-General Eden Bar Tal, and senior representatives of Israeli government agencies. The meetings were intended to build on earlier diplomatic engagements and identify opportunities for cooperation between public institutions and private companies.
The two countries also convened their first joint working group on water management, led on the Israeli side by the Israel Water Authority. The working group was established following a decision reached during Sa'ar's January visit to Astana.
Kazakhstan's extensive territory and varied climate have made efficient water management a national priority, particularly in agriculture and infrastructure. Israeli expertise in irrigation, water monitoring, and reducing water loss could provide opportunities for cooperation as Kazakhstan works to modernize its systems.
Israeli, Kazakh companies explore investments in critical minerals, cybersecurity
Alongside the diplomatic meetings, the Foreign Ministry and Israel Export Institute organized a bilateral business forum, in cooperation with the Israel Innovation Authority and the Manufacturers Association of Israel.
The forum brought together Israeli companies and members of the Kazakh delegation to explore opportunities in advanced technology, industry, and infrastructure. A separate roundtable focused on critical minerals, a sector of growing importance to global manufacturing, battery production, and renewable energy technologies.
Additional meetings involved Israeli organizations working in innovation, space technology, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity. Kazakhstan's government also reported that seven commercial documents were signed during the business forum, while discussions addressed direct air connections and possible visa-free travel arrangements.
The visit follows efforts to establish deeper technological ties between the countries. During Herzog's April visit, he toured Kazakhstan's alem.ai artificial intelligence center, where he was received by Madiyev and met representatives of the country's technology sector, as previously reported by The Jerusalem Post.
Kazakhstan's Abraham Accords membership strengthens strategic ties with Israel
The economic agreements also carry diplomatic significance in the context of Kazakhstan's participation in the Abraham Accords.
Kazakhstan announced its accession to the US-brokered framework on November 6, 2025, following a telephone conversation involving US President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The development expanded the initiative's reach into Central Asia, where Israel has maintained diplomatic relations with Kazakhstan since 1992.
Although the two countries already enjoyed established diplomatic ties, Kazakhstan's participation in the accords created an additional framework for economic engagement, technological partnerships, and regional cooperation.
In September 2026, Kazakhstan participated in a meeting of Abraham Accords countries and partner organizations in New York, where discussions focused on expanding practical cooperation between participating states. The meeting underscored Kazakhstan's potential role in connecting Israel and its regional partners with markets across Central Asia and the broader Eurasian region.
Elkin expressed confidence that the Abraham Accords would help deepen bilateral economic cooperation, particularly in sectors where Israeli technology and Kazakhstan's natural resources could complement one another.
Kazakhstan's uranium, copper and lithium resources attract strategic interest
Beyond the agreements signed in Jerusalem, Kazakhstan's economic importance lies in its substantial natural resources, energy production, and geographic position between Europe and Asia.
Dr. Anat Hochberg-Marom, a geopolitical analyst, highlighted these factors in a recent commentary examining Kazakhstan's growing role in the Abraham Accords and the wider international economy.
Hochberg-Marom described Kazakhstan as Central Asia's largest and most stable economy, citing a gross domestic product of approximately $301 billion and a 2025 growth forecast of 5.6%. These figures reflect the historical estimates cited in her analysis rather than updated 2026 economic data.
She also noted Kazakhstan's role as the world's leading uranium producer, accounting for roughly 40% of global output in 2024, as well as its production of copper and zinc and its significant tungsten and lithium resources.
These minerals have become increasingly important to international supply chains, particularly as governments and companies seek to secure materials used in batteries, renewable energy infrastructure, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing.
Kazakhstan's position between Europe, Asia opens new markets for Israeli companies
According to Hochberg-Marom, Kazakhstan's geographic position offers opportunities extending beyond bilateral trade with Israel.
As a major energy producer and transit country connecting Asia and Europe, Kazakhstan could play a larger role in regional logistics, manufacturing, and international supply chains. Its participation in the Abraham Accords could provide an additional platform for cooperation with Israel and other participating countries.
The analyst suggested that expanding regional partnerships could help attract further international investment into Kazakhstan's technology and industrial sectors, particularly in fields undergoing rapid modernization.
She pointed to investment initiatives involving approximately $1.1 billion in critical minerals development, including tungsten and lithium, as well as a reported $2 billion technology initiative involving OpenAI and Nvidia to develop artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Hochberg-Marom also cited approximately $70 billion in historical US investment in Kazakhstan's oil sector over three decades, arguing that new technology and mineral projects could support efforts to diversify the country's economy beyond traditional energy production. She presented the investment figures in her analysis, and they should not be treated as confirmation of newly signed agreements during Madiyev's visit.

articles.title: Zelensky says dozens dead, missing in Russian strike days before US talks - Free Malaysia Today
articles.summary: Zelensky says dozens dead, missing in Russian strike days before US talks  Free Malaysia Today
articles.full_text:
Russia pummelled Ukraine Monday and Tuesday after a rare truce between the enemies ended at the weekend, with the strikes dampening hopes for a breakthrough at US-led negotiations set for next week in Abu Dhabi.
Rescue operations were ongoing in the frontline southeastern village of Komyshuvakha, where Russian forces had struck a former school building that Ukraine said was being used to distribute aid every Monday.
“Just one strike killed 33 people. Five people were rescued, and more than 50 may still be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky said, describing it as “one of the largest Russian killings of this war”.
The attack hit hours after a ceasefire held for several days in the Kherson region, allowing for a rare humanitarian mission.
A Russian strike on a hospital in Kharkiv also wounded dozens Tuesday, Zelensky said, with Ukrainian authorities reporting another four dead across the country.
Zelensky, the Kremlin and Washington confirmed their negotiators will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10-11 for the first talks between all three sides since February.
Visiting Berlin Tuesday, Zelensky said he hoped that the gathering will pave the way for his meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” he told reporters.
Zelensky has consistently pushed for a meeting with Putin – who sent Russian troops over the border in 2022, unleashing Europe’s worst war since World War II.
Putin, however, has repeatedly refused face-to-face talks with Zelensky.
Speaking alongside Zelensky, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he saw no sign that Russia was willing to engage seriously in ending its invasion.
“It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement,” he said.
“I do not see that happening so far.”
‘Ukraine must be at the table’
Kyiv and its European allies have feared US President Donald Trump – who signed a diesel deal with Putin recently and who has criticised Zelensky – is siding with the Kremlin.
Merz said that if Trump invites Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, then Zelensky should be invited, too.
“If Ukraine is to be discussed, then the president of Ukraine must be at the table.”
Last week’s ceasefire in Kherson – brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump – had provided a glimmer of hope that a negotiated end to the conflict could be on the horizon.
Zelensky said Kyiv had offered Russia an extension of the ceasefire, but shortly afterwards Moscow unleashed deadly strikes.
“We proposed to Russia to prolong and expand the ceasefire,” Zelensky said.
“But in response, we got this, this kind of attack. New shelling, new strikes, new killings.”
Merz said that while the Kherson ceasefire could have served as “a model” for other truces, “Russia has so far stubbornly refused this.”
Talks in Brussels
“Our message to Russia is therefore clear: it is time to bring this war to an end,” Merz, who leads one of Ukraine’s main military and financial backers, said.
Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not want a temporary ceasefire in Ukraine and that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine by force.
Repeated Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in recent weeks have raised fears of another difficult winter ahead, and on Tuesday Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said supplies in the capital were “extremely difficult”.
Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials on Wednesday in Brussels.
Representatives from Ukraine, the United States, France, Germany, Britain, Nato and the World Bank will take part, the European Commission said.
In Russia, Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said nearly 500 drones heading towards the capital region were destroyed.
The strikes came as Britain and France announced that around 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will stage military drills in Poland this month in support of Ukraine.

articles.title: Why Armenia’s EU Membership Could Be Smoother Than Most Prospective Members - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Why Armenia’s EU Membership Could Be Smoother Than Most Prospective Members - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- After Russia’s inaction in the 2020–23 Karabakh conflicts, Pashinyan froze CSTO participation in 2024 and began diversifying defense imports toward India and France while deepening U.S. ties.
- In 2024–25 Armenia advanced EU accession legislation, prompting Russian import bans and hostile rhetoric.
- The absence of active territorial disputes and ongoing reforms are cited as advantages over other candidates, though elections and residual Russian influence remain risks.
Armenia, after decades of Russian influence, has made strides in democratic reforms and branching out to alternative partners in trade, technology, and defense. Over the past several years, Armenia’s ruling government, led by Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, has expressed interest in future European Union membership.
Yerevan’s potential accension will face hurdles; as it has been under Moscow’s influence for decades, reforming full democratic control remains paramount to the country’s future. Amid the diversification process, Armenia continues to transform into a solidified Western partner with key agreements with the U.S. and stronger ties with Europe.
Initial Russian-Economic Bloc and Breakdown in Relations
Against the backdrop of the dissolution of the USSR, Armenia gained its independence from the Soviet Union, albeit in a weakened and precarious state. Armenia’s democratic institutions were initially flawed, with a lack of structural safeguards, which would be seen up until the Velvet Revolution.
Immediately after independence, Armenia would fight a major war with Azerbaijan over the Karabakh region, which also desired autonomy and self-determination. The Karabakh region, historically with an Armenian majority and Armenian architecture, was transferred to the then Azerbaijani SSR by Josef Stalin, who wished to ignite ethnic tensions and quell nationalism within the USSR.
The First Karabakh war ended in an Armenian military victory. Still, a Russian-mediated ceasefire left the dispute unresolved—particularly due to Azerbaijani refugees and the status of the breakaway state of Artsakh, which was supported but not annexed by Armenia. Moscow would be Yerevan’s closest ally at the time, allowing Armenia to join the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), but this allyship would be tested amid the Velvet Revolution.
During the Velvet Revolution, Armenians removed the pro-Russian bloc that was close to longtime autocrat Vladimir Putin, which the Kremlin took as a spiteful act akin to Euromaidan in Ukraine and the Georgian protests. When Azerbaijan initiated the Second Karabakh war in 2020, Russia did not respond to Armenia’s request for assistance, and the resulting armed conflict saw Baku recapture much of the region from the Armenian army and Artsakh militias.
Russia would gain a foothold in the South Caucasus in 2020 it previously had lost thirty years ago from the collapse of the USSR via a peacekeeping contingent in the Karabakh region as over 120,000 Armenians remained under threat. However, this peacekeeping mission would prove hollow and set the stage for a major split between Yerevan and Moscow.
Armenia’s Western Pivot and EU Aspirations
In mid-September 2022, Azerbaijan would initiate large-scale artillery fire against Armenia proper. Several hundred troops on both sides would be killed in less than three days, with the United States mediating a ceasefire.
Despite a CSTO member in Armenia being attacked in its non-disputed territory, no member of the alliance took action to defend Yerevan, Russia included. Due to the inaction, Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan openly criticized the CSTO and slowly started a process of disengaging Yerevan from the mutual defense organization.
In February 2024, Pashinyan froze Armenia’s participation in CSTO a year after Azerbaijan launched one more major military operation in Karabakh in 2023 that saw the expulsion of over 100,000 Armenians and cultural desecration of ancient Armenian artifacts. Pashinyan would later state intentions to eventually leave CSTO as Armenia would branch out its dependency away from Russia.
Armenia is diversifying its defense imports away from Russia, increasing procurements from countries such as India and France. Starting with the outgoing Biden administration, Armenia was also upgraded towards a strategic comprehensive partnership with the United States, which continued to expand during Yerevan’s Western pivot.
Armenia’s Potential EU Ascension
On September 9th, 2024, Nikol Pashinyan acknowledged that starting Yerevan’s process towards European Union (EU) accension was a key policy of his government. Several months later, on March 26th, 2025, the Armenian parliament put forth a legislature called the EU Integration Act for future membership aspirations.
For the past year, Yerevan’s government has been engaging in domestic and democratic reforms to make the looming EU accession process smoother. For instance, Pashinyan’s government will expect opposition towards a Western pivot, as some of the opposing blocs maintain good ties with Russia, which could enact information and hybrid warfare against Armenia when its process begins.
Russia has already reacted to Armenia’s EU aspirations with ire by lobbying against Yerevan’s current Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) membership. In a form of sanctions and economic coercion, the Kremlin enacted bans on Armenian imports, with media figures and Duma members exacerbating rhetoric similar to that against Ukraine after Euromaidan. Despite the economic coercion, Armenia is unlikely to abandon EU aspirations, as over-reliance on Russia led to the country’s isolation from better-performing Western markets at a time when Yerevan needed outside support the most between 2020 and 2023.
Why Yerevan’s Prospects Could be Less Turbulent than Other Prospects
During Armenia’s preparations for EU accession, there are a handful of countries that are either in the process of negotiations or are in an indefinite standstill due to various reasons that involve other members of the European Union.Currently, Albania, Georgia, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Turkey, Ukraine, and Bosnia and Herzegovina are in the candidacy phase. However, only a handful of these countries will likely receive future membership in the next several years.
Montenegro is likely the next member of the European Union, as Podgorica has checked off everything it needs for future membership. Georgia and Moldova are currently suffering from pro-Russian movements and political crises which are amplified by the Kremlin’s informational warfare strategy. Ukraine, currently engaged in Europe’s largest war faces upheavals due to the ongoing conflict with Russia’s invasion.
Albania and Serbia are both dealing with political turmoil stemming from corruption that brings frequent protests to both countries, and North Macedonia is only four years into negotiations. Both Turkey and Bosnia and Herzegovina are embroiled in delicate situations that could have wider implications.
Turkey currently has a five-decade military occupation over the northern regions of Cyprus, and Nicosia is an EU member. Alongside Greece, which is a mutual treaty ally of Nicosia, Ankara’s EU aspirations are likely to remain in purgatory until a full resolution of Cyprus’ frozen conflict is mended.
Bosnia and Herzegovina faces a renewed separatist movement from one of its internal entities, the Republika Srpska (RS). The RS has stepped up lobbying efforts with U.S. officials in the Trump administration to lobby towards independence, which not only threatens Bosnia and Herzegovina’s EU accession, but also the Dayton Accords that could bring various factions back into ethnic armed conflicts that still scar the Balkans to this day.
Armenia currently has no open conflicts or disputes, particularly as Pashinyan offered territorial proposals of acknowledgement and land swaps to Azerbaijan. Yerevan is continuing to implement democratic reforms and is increasingly leaving Russian-led blocs, which means EU integration will be smoother. Still, Yerevan cannot remain complacent, as by the time the country is formally in negotiations, future elections will take place, and the pro-Western Civil Contract party could face future challenges to the EU aspirations.
Overall, Armenia’s trajectory from an obscure country surrounded by enemies and heavy Russian influence is now brighter, with a freer market democracy that can branch out to various countries for technology, economic trade, and defense instead of solely relying on the Kremlin. European Union membership aspirations can help Yerevan not only grow but also bring needed investments to the South Caucasus.
