articles.title: Russia, Mozambique Bilateral Relations: October 2026 Update - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia, Mozambique Bilateral Relations: October 2026 Update  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
Mozambique and Russia have maintained close political and diplomatic ties for decades, President Daniel Francisco Chapo has said, highlighting the longstanding partnership between the two nations.
Speaking during his visit to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit, Chapo noted the relationship dates back to Mozambique’s struggle for independence, when Moscow provided military and security assistance. He stressed that cooperation in these areas continues today.
“Mozambique and Russia already enjoy excellent political and diplomatic relations,” the president said.
Chapo said his visit to Russia was intended to strengthen economic cooperation and attract new investment, building on the countries’ established political ties. He noted that bilateral trade has increased but that considerable room remains for further growth.
The president identified agriculture, industry, mineral resources, energy, digital transformation, tourism, transport, and logistics among the sectors where Mozambique hopes to attract Russian companies.
Mozambique is also seeking Russian partners to develop gas pipelines, power plants, and fertilizer production facilities, Chapo said, adding that the countries are “working together to find solutions and develop these projects.”
Security cooperation in bilateral affairs features prominently in the relationship. Chapo said Mozambican military and law enforcement cadets are currently receiving training at Russian academies. The president also confirmed that Mozambique is discussing possible cooperation with Russia to address terrorism in the African state. He pointed to Moscow’s counterterrorism experience and said the two sides are exploring potential solutions through their existing security partnership.
Mozambique’s northern Cabo Delgado province has faced an insurgency by Islamic State-linked militants since 2017. The violence has killed thousands and displaced more than a million people, prompting the deployment of Rwandan troops in 2021 to support government forces.
Russia and Mozambique signed a memorandum on road construction, maintenance, and toll-road management during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on October 28. According to Russia’s Transport Ministry, the two countries also discussed establishing a direct shipping route and involving Russian companies in railway projects.
Mozambique’s economy remains heavily reliant on natural resources, with extractive industries driving growth. Agriculture, which employs over 72% of the population. Mozambique’s exports are dominated by large projects in the extractive sector (coal, gas, rubies, and heavy sands), accounting for 60% of overall exports. Overall, the main manufacturing products in Mozambique include wheat flour; food; beverages; aluminium; petroleum products; textiles; cement; glass; and tobacco.
Mozambique is a member of the African Continental Free commerce Area (AfCFTA), which provides free trade on 95% on all African goods transported across the continent. Mozambique is also a member of the Southern African Development Community, with whom Russia signed a cooperation and development agreement last week.
Mozambique has a population of 34 million and a GDP (PPP) of US$46 billion. GDP per capita (PPP) is US$ 2,383. Mozambique’s real GDP growth for 2026 is projected to be between 0.5% and 2.1%. This slow growth is due to severe floods, the shutdown of the MOZAL aluminium smelter, and impacts on farming. Future growth relies heavily on natural gas projects, an area where Russia can be of development assistance.
Mozambique took part in Russia’s ‘Great African Expedition’ designed to assess fish stocks on its Indian Ocean coastline, with a view to developing maritime and fish processing joint ventures. During the 2026 Russia-Africa summit plenary session, President Chapo invited Russian investors to collaborate in mechanized agriculture and industry, energy, infrastructure, and transport logistics, as well as the blue economy and digital transformation.
Mozambique’s trade with Russia is about US$160 million, and according to President Putin, speaking during the 2026 Russia-Africa summit, it has doubled during 8M 2026. Trade is mostly agriculture-based, with Russia exporting wheat and fertilizers and Mozambique exporting tea. Both countries are aiming to increase commerce and tourism through new infrastructure and transport agreements.

articles.title: OTS Summit in Ankara: Türkiye Looks to Strengthen Its Position as Central Asia Competes for Transit Routes - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: OTS Summit in Ankara: Türkiye Looks to Strengthen Its Position as Central Asia Competes for Transit Routes  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived in Ankara on October 28, the day he delivered his annual State of the Nation Address, in which he announced plans to expand transport routes between China and Europe. On October 30, he will attend the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Turkey is preparing to take over the organization’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and Central Asian countries are seeking to accelerate freight transportation across the Caspian Sea.
Behind the shared rhetoric of Turkic unity lie specific economic interests. Kazakhstan is building railways and expanding its capacity to handle transit cargo from China. Azerbaijan is developing Caspian ports and transport infrastructure in the South Caucasus. Turkey wants to attract more freight moving between China and Europe through Central Asia, increasing its role as a transit hub.
A unified route looks much simpler on a political map than it does in the daily operations of transport companies. Between China and Europe, cargo crosses several borders, is transferred from trains to ships and back, undergoes customs clearance, and is subject to tariffs set by different operators.
Interest in alternative Eurasian transport routes has grown since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but the competition extends beyond freight. Ankara is looking to strengthen its political presence in Central Asia, where Russia and China retain considerable influence.
Summit events begin on October 29 with a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers, chaired by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. The nation’s presidents will meet on the following day. Participants are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, discuss investment, energy, digitalization, security, and appoint a new OTS secretary-general.
Tokayev and Kazakhstan’s Route to Europe
Tokayev’s visit to Turkey follows directly after his State of the Nation Address, much of which focused on infrastructure, including plans to open the 272-kilometer Bakhty–Ayagoz railway in 2027. The line is expected to add 20 million metric tons of annual freight capacity between Kazakhstan and China.
Tokayev also discussed construction of the Aral–Caspian highway. The project would establish a new transport connection between western and central Kazakhstan. According to government estimates, it could shorten certain freight routes between China and Europe by approximately 1,000 kilometers and reduce delivery times by up to three days.
Both projects are part of a broader effort to increase Kazakhstan’s revenue from international logistics. The country currently earns a substantial share of its transit revenue directly from freight transportation. Developing warehouses, terminals, processing facilities, and distribution centers could generate additional income.
Turkey occupies an important position in this network. An overland branch of the Middle Corridor passes through its territory en route to European markets; the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway connects Azerbaijan to Turkey’s rail network through Georgia.
On the sidelines of the Ankara summit, Turkish business associations plan to discuss border crossing operations, transportation costs, and the development of the Middle Corridor.
Transport geography, however, does not fit neatly within the OTS’s political boundaries. Georgia, through which the railway connecting Azerbaijan and Turkey passes, is not a member of the organization. China, which generates a substantial share of potential freight traffic, also remains outside it.
The Caspian section presents additional challenges. The capacity of the ports of Aktau, Kuryk, and Baku depends on the availability of vessels, weather conditions, and coordination of railway schedules. A delay along one section can eliminate the advantage of a shorter overland route.
Ankara Expands Its Influence, Astana Draws Boundaries
Turkey has steadily strengthened its ties with Central Asia through trade, education, defense cooperation, and infrastructure projects. The OTS brings these areas together within a permanent framework for high-level negotiations.
But the five member states do not share a unified foreign policy.
Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan belong to the Eurasian Economic Union alongside Russia, Belarus, and Armenia. Both countries are also members of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, while Turkey is a NATO member, and Uzbekistan maintains a policy of nonparticipation in military blocs.
Central Asian members also balance their ties with Turkey against relationships with China, Russia, and the European Union. Those outside partnerships complicate efforts to forge a common OTS foreign policy.
At the May summit in Turkestan, Tokayev rejected portraying the organization as a military or geopolitical alliance, emphasizing practical cooperation, a position analysts interpreted as evidence of differing visions within the OTS.
Turkey’s upcoming chairmanship brings these differences back into focus. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan wants to increase the OTS’s international standing, while its Central Asian members are pursuing closer cooperation without limiting their wider diplomatic and economic partnerships.
Uzbekistan Seeks Leadership of the Secretariat
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is set to visit Turkey on October 29–30, with Tashkent announcing plans for discussions covering trade, investment, transport logistics, tourism, environmental issues, and education.
Uzbekistan joined the OTS in 2019, after the organization’s other current members. According to Uzbekistan’s government, it has since proposed more than 85 initiatives across various areas.
The summit is expected to appoint a new secretary-general. Mehmet Seyfettin Erol, president of the Ankara Center for Crisis and Policy Studies (ANKASAM), anticipates an Uzbek representative taking the role for the first time. Such an appointment would strengthen Tashkent’s presence within the organization’s permanent institutions.
In his assessment, cooperation between Turkey and Uzbekistan could accelerate the organization’s work in trade, investment, energy, digitalization, and transportation.
Uzbekistan is seeking new transport links to international markets. As a landlocked country, it relies on neighboring states and transit partners to move goods westward.
However, Tashkent and Astana have competing transit interests. The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, could divert some freight from routes through Kazakhstan. Uzbekistan proposes linking the railway to the Middle Corridor, but the routes would still compete for cargo.
The OTS can help coordinate these projects, but its secretary-general cannot settle competing national priorities. Decisions on infrastructure financing and transport policy remain with national governments.
A Shared History Has Not Created a Common Market
The Organization of Turkic States was established in 2009 as the Cooperation Council of Turkic Speaking States and adopted its current name in 2021.
Its full members are Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey, and Uzbekistan. Hungary, Turkmenistan, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization have observer status. Northern Cyprus is recognized as an independent state only by Turkey, and its participation in the OTS has been a source of friction, according to analysts.
In recent years, the OTS has established several economic mechanisms, including the Turkic Investment Fund. Members are also expanding cooperation among customs authorities, transport operators, and business associations. But there is no common market within the organization. Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan follow the customs rules of the Eurasian Economic Union, while the other members operate under their own trade regimes and international agreements.
Yaşar Sarı, a professor at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University and director of the Heydar Aliyev Center for Eurasian Studies, considers strengthening existing institutions more important than expanding the OTS or attempting to form a new geopolitical bloc. In an interview with CASPIA Lab, he advocated developing economic integration, transport cooperation, and regional coordination.
The OTS can help finance projects and coordinate negotiations, but national governments retain control over transport policy. Its members also have commitments to partners outside the organization, limiting how far they can act together. Agreeing on a joint statement is easier than negotiating lower freight charges or shorter border delays across several countries.

Europe and Central Asia pavilion showcases heritage and new technologies
At Rome’s historic Circo Massimo, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) hosted the Europe and Central Asia Pavilion of its global exhibition “From Seeds to Foods.” Held over five days from 30 October 2026, the pavilion brought together farmers, food producers, researchers, governments, businesses, civil society organizations and young innovators to show how agricultural traditions and cutting-edge technologies can work together.
The pavilion assembled more than 90 exhibitors from over 25 countries, and the global exhibition drew more than 25,000 visitors, according to FAO’s regional office. The event used the theme “Rooted in Nature, Powered by People” to explore how nature, traditional knowledge, science and investment can support more sustainable and resilient agrifood systems.
Building agrifood systems through “science and innovation”
A core focus of the pavilion was how research and technology can complement local knowledge. Interactive demonstrations and short talks featured examples including biotechnology and precision irrigation, as well as approaches linked to circular economy and new machinery.
Among the exhibitors, Italy-based Orange Fiber demonstrated how by-products from citrus juice production can be transformed into textile fibres, describing a model that links agriculture to circular materials. The company showcased its partnership with textile producer Lenzing to illustrate how circular economy approaches can reduce waste and open innovation pathways beyond the food sector.
Research institutions also highlighted future food priorities. Italy’s Council for Agricultural Research and Economics (CREA) presented developments in wholegrain food processing, while Belgium’s Ghent University explored underutilized crops and alternative proteins, including a presentation connecting food science to social media communication. Biotization presented applications of biotechnology in food and agriculture, positioning biotechnology as another research area with potential to support transformation in agrifood systems.
Technological innovation was not limited to processing. WES TRADE, through its IRRIGOPTIMAL® precision irrigation and Agricolus, presented digital farming approaches aimed at supporting agricultural decision-making and more efficient resource use. Ukraine’s GF Robotics displayed autonomous farming technologies intended to help address safety challenges for farmers working in conflict-affected areas, according to the pavilion programme.
Protecting natural resources and valuing traditional knowledge
Alongside new technologies, the pavilion emphasized the importance of protecting the natural resources that underpin food production. The Save the Soil Global Movement contributed perspectives on soil conservation, linking technological innovation with safeguarding healthy, productive soils.
FAO also placed farmers and rural knowledge at the center of the visitor experience. The “Tree of Life – Voices from the Field” installation—described by FAO as a wooden art installation reflecting the circular economy—elevated farmers’ experiences and highlighted their role in conserving biodiversity, sustaining rural livelihoods and transforming agrifood systems.
An interactive beehive display and honey tastings led by beekeepers from Association Api Sparse drew attention to pollinators and the way healthy ecosystems support agricultural production and food security.
Celebrating food heritage, pastoralists and women farmers
Food culture featured prominently during the five-day event through tastings of regional products across Europe and Central Asia, including olive oil, honey, breads, dairy products and wines. The programme included an olive oil masterclass and tastings of products promoted through FAO’s One Country One Priority Product initiative, which highlights distinctive local foods as potential economic opportunities for producers and rural communities.
The pavilion also recognized people who sustain agricultural landscapes. On 10 October, activities were described as celebrating the 2026 International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, and the contributions of pastoralist communities to biodiversity, rural livelihoods and food traditions. FAO also highlighted the 2026 International Year of the Woman Farmer by focusing on women’s roles in safeguarding traditional seed varieties, preserving food knowledge and driving entrepreneurship and innovation.
One listed exhibitor was Serbia’s 100 Women Winery, a cooperative founded by women who planted vineyards near Niš. FAO described it as bringing women from different backgrounds together to produce wine, building on local winemaking traditions while creating opportunities in a sector FAO described as male-dominated.
A shared message: connecting people, knowledge and innovation
Across the pavilion, FAO’s messaging tied agrifood transformation to both inherited knowledge and scientific advances. FAO Assistant Director-General and Regional Representative for Europe and Central Asia Viorel Gutu said in relation to the event that “Science and innovation come together with traditional knowledge, preserving what works, adapting to change and finding new ways to produce food sustainably.”
In FAO’s account, the Europe and Central Asia Pavilion used the journey from seeds to foods to emphasize that outcomes depend on farmers, food producers, researchers, and partnerships working together. By connecting nature, knowledge, science and innovation, the pavilion aimed to illustrate pathways toward more efficient, inclusive, resilient and sustainable agrifood systems, with an explicit focus on leaving no one behind.
Key Details
- Initiative/Programme: Europe and Central Asia Pavilion of FAO’s “From Seeds to Foods” exhibition
- Lead organization: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
- Partners: Listed exhibitors and collaborators included Orange Fiber, Lenzing, CREA (Council for Agricultural Research and Economics), Ghent University, Save the Soil Global Movement, WES TRADE, Agricolus, GF Robotics, Association Api Sparse, Ristorante Georgiano Aisi, and 100 Women Winery (as an exhibitor); additional partners were named generally as farmers, research institutions, governments, businesses, civil society organizations and young innovators
- Funding amount: Not specified in the source
- Geographic focus: Europe and Central Asia pavilion at Circo Massimo in Rome; exhibitors from over 25 countries
- Target groups: Farmers, food producers, researchers, young innovators, civil society organizations, governments, and visitors to the exhibition
- Duration/timeline: Five days (event page dated 30/10/2026; specific closing date not stated in the excerpt)
- Expected reach/outcomes: More than 90 exhibitors from over 25 countries; global exhibition welcomed more than 25,000 visitors (reach figures stated by FAO)
Why This Matters
For NGO leaders and development practitioners, FAO’s Europe and Central Asia pavilion underscores how agrifood system programming is increasingly framed as an integration challenge—pairing innovation with traditional knowledge and stronger environmental safeguards. The event’s emphasis on soil conservation, pollinator health, and safer farming in conflict-affected contexts points to program design priorities that remain relevant for partners working on climate resilience, livelihoods and food security.
The pavilion also illustrates opportunities for collaboration across sectors and roles—linking research institutions, technology providers, women’s organizations and civil society—while highlighting international themes such as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists and the International Year of the Woman Farmer. For grantmakers and fundraisers, the showcased breadth of actors suggests a continued donor and stakeholder interest in “connected ecosystems” approaches rather than stand-alone interventions.

TASHKENT, November 3. /Dunyo IA/. Professor Komil Rashidov, Head of the Sector of Legislation in the Economic Sphere at the Institute of Legislation and Legal Policy under the President of Uzbekistan, commented for the Dunyo IA on the outcomes of the working visit of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to Türkiye and his participation in the Organization of Turkic States Summit:
- Consistent implementation of New Uzbekistan’s foreign policy, alongside the regular and effective conduct of bilateral and multilateral negotiations in political, economic, cultural, and humanitarian spheres based on the interests of the people and the state, aligns with the constitutional foundations of foreign policy.
Operating on the principle of “objective—action—result”, economic diplomacy of New Uzbekistan is filled with concrete substance, including at high-level multilateral diplomacy platforms, aimed at expanding mutually beneficial bilateral cooperation.
Thus, within the framework of the working visit of the President of Uzbekistan to Türkiye on October 29–30th to participate in the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Ankara, high-level bilateral meetings were also held, during which issues of further strengthening the Uzbek-Turkish comprehensive strategic partnership relations, particularly in political-diplomatic, trade-economic and cultural-humanitarian spheres, were discussed.
Following the negotiations, Leaders of Uzbekistan and Türkiye signed an Agreement on the Establishment of the High-Level Business Support Council. A number of bilateral documents were also signed aimed at further expanding trade and economic cooperation, creating favorable conditions for business circles and providing them with legal assistance, as well as ensuring the effective protection of citizens' social rights.
It should be noted that the established High-Level Business Support Council is a new format for supporting comprehensive trade and economic cooperation between the two countries. Its activities are aimed at providing large-scale support to entrepreneurs, promptly eliminating barriers, and elevating the bilateral trade and economic partnership to a qualitatively new level.
New Council and the existing Joint Intergovernmental Commission will collectively address the task set by the heads of state to bring trade turnover to $5 billion, including through expanding the product list within the Framework Agreement on Preferential Trade and broadening the portfolio of promising projects.
These economic interaction structures, including Uzbek-Turkish Business Council, will serve as powerful tools within the activities of the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council led by the heads of both states.
Meetings of the head of our state in Ankara with representatives of leading Turkish companies, during which promising avenues for investment cooperation were reviewed, testify to the business community's trust in the reforms implemented in the country:
Additional investment projects to modernize the “SamAvto” enterprise in Samarkand, expand its production capacities and increase product export volumes were discussed with “Anadolu Group”;
“Evyap Holding” expressed readiness to further expand mutually beneficial cooperation in the manufacturing of personal hygiene products and cosmetics, and to implement a new project launched in the Uzbek-Turkish industrial zone “OSTIM Global”;
Issues concerning the further expansion of projects in renewable energy, geology and the mining industry, infrastructure, establishment of an electric vehicle charging station network, as well as the food industry were discussed jointly with “Eksim Holding”;
“OYAK” expressed interest in implementing joint investment projects in the chemical industry, geology, and construction in New Uzbekistan, as well as readiness to actively participate in the construction of residential complexes and external infrastructure facilities in New Tashkent.
Comprehensive strategic partnership between the two states, Constitution, legislation on foreign economic and investment activities and the provisions of the Agreement on the Reciprocal Promotion and Protection of Investments with Türkiye serve as the legal foundation for implementing the agreements reached in Ankara with leading Turkish business circles.
Following these meetings, Head of our State emphasized the significant role and contribution of business circles to the consistently developing strategic partnership relations of our country with Türkiye.
Continuation of practical cooperation in economic diplomacy across new avenues was also proposed within the multilateral format.
Thus, in his address at the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, Head of Uzbekistan put forward a proposal to adopt the “Turkic World – 100” Program, encompassing one hundred strategic joint investment and industrial projects, including the processing of rare minerals and the localization of manufacturing equipment for green energy. Attention was focused on the importance of attracting resources from the Turkic Investment Fund, which also accumulates the financial assets of Uzbekistan and international financial institutions for the implementation of these projects.
Other important initiatives of the Uzbek side include proposals:
• on the development of a multilateral Treaty “On Mutual Legal Assistance in Commercial Matters”, which is essential for protecting the interests of entrepreneurs, as well as the creation of a digital platform designated for the electronic exchange of legal assistance requests and documents;
• on the establishment of the “Network of Logistics Centers of the Turkic States” and ensuring its joint management, which will allow expanding the participation of the organization's member states in international freight transportation and logistics, as well as increasing economic integration;
• on the creation of the “Turkic Tourism Alliance” to expand tourism potential, as well as the development of a multilateral agreement providing for the simplification of mutual travel of citizens and the expansion of opportunities for travel using ID cards.
Historical significance of the high-level negotiations held, the signed bilateral and multilateral documents, and the business meetings within the framework of the working visit to Türkiye open a new chapter in our country's economic diplomacy. They create the necessary conditions for filling the Uzbek-Turkish mutually beneficial trade, economic and investment interaction with concrete achievements, as well as for further expanding multifaceted cooperation among the member states of the Organization of Turkic States for the sake of Turkic solidarity.

What you need to know
This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of the latest developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, November 2.
- At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center in Zaporizhzhia region
- Russia, Ukraine hit by cyberattacks after humanitarian truce ends in Russian-occupied Oleshky
- Zelenskyy offers to stop hitting Russian refineries if the US delivers Patriot missiles

Multinational force to hold first excersise in Poland
A force of about 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will hold the first exercise of a new multinational force in support of Ukraine, the UK and France said.
The force is only to be deployed in the case of a ceasefire that would end the war between Kyiv and Moscow, with its aim being supporting Ukraine's army in securing the country.
"The exercise will allow the testing of the speed and efficiency at which several nations can deploy forces on land, sea and air to support Ukraine once hostilities have finished," a joint statement by the two countries reads.
With Russia not showing any intention of agreeing peace, the move could further antagonize Moscow.
The exercise will take place between November 9 and 22 in Poland, not far from the country's Ukraine border.
Russian, Ukrainian representatives to meet in Abu Dhabi — Witkoff
A trilateral meeting between officials from the US, Russia and Ukraine will take place in Abu Dhabi next week, US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff said.
According to Witkoff, the US will mediate "working-level" negotiations between Russia and Ukraine on November 10 and 11, in a bid of "advancing President Trump's mission to end the war."
"Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace," Witkoff posted on his X account, adding that meetings will also take place with representatives from NATO, Germany, the UK and the EU.
The goal, Witkoff said, is a "comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come."
Meanwhile, a senior US official told Reuters that Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the lead U.S. negotiators, are expected to represent the US in Abu Dhabi.
Zaporizhzhia: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center
At least 26 people were killed and five more injured on Monday when the Russian air force launched repeated strikes on a school which was functioning as an aid distribution center in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia.
The multiple attacks, in which Russian planes reportedly launched more than 10 glide bombs, took place in the village of Komyshuvakha, about 35 kilometers (31 miles) east of the city of Zaporizhzhia and a dozen kilometers away from the frontline.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attacks as "utterly horrific" and accused Russia of being well aware of the humanitarian purpose of the site.
"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on social media.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that every week, local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid at that very location."
Ukrainian emergency services said two members of a rescue crew were among the dead after falling victim to the so-called "double-tap" strike in which a location is targeted again with the aim of hitting first responders.
The attacks came less than 24 hours after a localized six-day humanitarian ceasefire in and around the town of Oleshky in the neighboring region of Kherson had expired.
Zelenskyy said the temporary truce could potentially have led to further steps toward a possible deal to end the ongoing Russian invasion, but said after Monday's strikes:
"This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de-escalation or any real justice... With these killings, Russia has sent a completely opposite signal; Russia is counting on further killings."
The Zaporizhzhia region has been targeted repeatedly for months by heavy Russian airstrikes.
Ukraine says Russia used ceasefire to rearm, rotate troops, Kremlin says 'it's normal practice'
Ukraine's General Staff on Monday blasted Russia's actions during a six-day humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, saying the Kremlin had used the break in fighting to rearm its forces and rotate troops in the front-line area.
In a social media post on X, the General Staff wrote: "Defense Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," adding, "The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."
Residents in the Kherson region were warned to be vigilant and told to pay attention to air raid sirens, noting that an intensification of attacks was to be expected after Russia used the brief pause to "strengthen its capabilities."
In Moscow, the Kremlin brushed off the critique, saying Ukraine, "could have used the ceasefire to re-group as well," calling such activity, "normal practice."
Kyiv region sees emergency power outages
Ukraine energy provider DTEK on Monday said that emergency power cuts had been initiated in Kyiv and the surrounding region at the request of national grid operator Ukrenergo.
The outages follow Russian attacks in central Ukraine that left over 200,000 Ukrainians in the area without power over the weekend.
DTEK had previously announced that, "equipment in the region has been seriously damaged due to enemy attacks," adding that energy workers were trying to "restore power to critical infrastructure facilities."
The attacks follow the Kremlin's playbook of seeking to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure, especially in cold months, in an attempt to break the will of Ukraine's citizens defending themselves against Russia's invasion by "weaponizing winter."
Ukraine says it evacuated more than 150 from Kherson region before ceasefire expired
Ukraine's military has said that about 170 people were evacuated from the Kherson region (news agencies cite numbers ranging from 167 to 180) before a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired at midnight (Moscow time, 2100 GMT) on Sunday.
No resumption of hostilities was immediately reported after what was the longest pause in fighting since Russian forces invaded in 2022.
Kherson's regional governor on Sunday urged residents remaining behind to avoid "red zones" where he said the threat of Russian strikes "remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
Kherson has been subjected to drones attacks, shelling, glide bombs and airdropped mines for nearly five years.
In all, nearly 800 people were reportedly evacuated from the region during the temporary ceasefire, with residents shuttled to Russian-annexed Crimea, then to the Russia town of Anapa, before being flown to Belarus and then Ukraine.
Among those evacuated were 22 children and 21 individuals requiring mobility assistance said Ukraine's army.
US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV — both of whom were reportedly involved in securing the pause in fighting — praised cooperation between the sides, voicing hope that such work might lay the groundwork for a broader peace.
Before Russia launched its illegal invasion on February 24, 2022, and took control of 70% of Kherson, the area was home to more than one million people. Now it is estimated that about 140,000 remain.
Russia hits military facility, cargo vessel, in Ukraine's Odesa
Russia's forces struck a military facility in Ukraine's Odesa region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Telegram on Monday.
The statement added that a cargo vessel, which the ministry claimed was used for military purposes, was also hit 58 kilometers (36  miles) south of the Black Sea port city of Odesa.
Separately, news agency Reuters cited an official in Odesa as saying that four people had been injured in a Russian attack.
US reportedly pushing to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine
The United States is backing a quick resumption of Russian natural gas exports to Europe via pipelines crossing Ukraine as part of talks aimed at securing an energy ceasefire before winter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing US, European and Ukrainian officials.
The proposal involves selling Russian gas via a US intermediary to circumvent European sanctions, the report said, adding that it was mooted by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September.
DW could not immediately verify the report.
Russia's share in European gas supply has declined to about 11% now from 45% on the eve of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The European Union currently aims to completely phase out Russian gas imports by the end of 2027. And EU leaders have said they don't want to go back to relying on Russia for energy supplies.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine will stop refinery strikes if US sends Patriot missiles
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.
Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News, Zelenskyy said he had had "different and several" conversations with Trump and his team on the issue.
"We asked that we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he said.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid," Zelenskyy added.

articles.title: Russia bombs aid centre and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 26, officials say, World News - AsiaOne.com
articles.summary: Russia bombs aid centre and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 26, officials say, World News  AsiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday (Nov 2), killing 26 people, Ukrainian officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in a post on X that strikes first targeted a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid and then took aim at a nearby shelter.
"This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation," Zelenskiy said.
The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country's south. The limited ceasefire agreement had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas in Russian-occupied territory.
"There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible," Zelenskiy said. "With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings."
Zelenskiy later said in an address to the nation that Ukraine was expecting Russia to escalate its attacks at a time when the country is facing a shortage of missiles needed to defend itself.
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used flashlights to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. About 20 people are considered missing and the death toll could rise, these officials say.
Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
In other areas of Ukraine, authorities reported multiple Russian drone attacks that injured at least 17 people.
After cyberattacks, false alerts sent in Ukraine and Russia
Earlier, residents of Ukraine and Russia had received phony emergency alerts from government-run mobile apps that were hacked, authorities in both countries said. The phony alerts in Ukraine included a warning about an imminent nuclear threat.
It was not clear if the cyberattacks late Sunday in Ukraine and early Monday in Russia were related. Ukraine said its mobile app, which residents rely on to seek safety from Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being temporarily suspended. Russian authorities said efforts to restore its emergency alert mobile app were ongoing.
A Russian Telegram channel with links to the country's security services said Monday that a hacking group, Hitcore, claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian emergency alert system. The Associated Press did not independently verify the claim, and the affiliations or motivations of the purported hackers remained unclear.
The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv -—were written in English, Russian and Ukrainian. The English language alerts contained spelling and grammatical errors.
One of the messages, written in Russian, said: "Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming," a reference to a Russian ballistic missile.
There was little indication the fake alerts caused panic in Ukraine. Instead, there was a flood of humorous posts online, with social media users sharing photos of their pets relaxing and apocalypse-themed images generated by artificial intelligence.
A spokesman for Ukraine's air force command, Yurii Ihnat, said in a television interview that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defence operations. The government urged people to monitor other emergency channels on social media while the cyberattack was being addressed.
In Russia, the Emergency Situations Ministry said in a statement that hackers sent a false alert through its app at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time on Monday across 33 of Russia's 89 regions. It did not say who it believed carried out the attack.
The ministry sought to reassure Russians by noting that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.
"All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Limited ceasefire ends in Kherson region
As the ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region came to an end on Monday, Ukraine's general staff said that Russia's military had used the pause in fighting to bolster its drone defences and replenish ammunition supplies.
The brief pause in fighting, which began on Oct 27, was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.
Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.
Russia's Ministry of Defence said Monday that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight. The head of Russia's Samara region, Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement that local air defences were repelling an aerial attack, but did not give further details.
Independent Russian media outlets later reported that Ukrainian drones had targeted one of Europe's largest oil transport hubs in Samara.
Russia-Ukraine negotiations planned for next week
US President Donald Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, posted on X that talks the US will mediate between Russia and Ukraine are set to take place Nov 10-11 in Abu Dhabi, focusing on postwar security arrangements, deescalation and humanitarian efforts.
Russia had agreed last month to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war, setting up the first such talks since February, but no date had been set.
Witkoff added that US mediators also would meet this week in Brussels with officials from France, Germany, the UK, the European Union and NATO to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and the larger region as well as support for rebuilding the war-torn country.
Source: Associated Press

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine ceasefire expires: Kherson region residents brace for new strikes ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: Russia-Ukraine ceasefire expires: Kherson region residents brace for new strikes ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
Residents of the Kherson region are preparing for the end of a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which has allowed the evacuation of civilians and the delivery of food, water and medicine to the frontline town of Oleshki. The ceasefire was agreed for Oleshki and the surrounding areas and represents the largest such pause between Kiev and Moscow since the start of a full-scale Russian invasion in 2022.
The White House said Melania Trump helped negotiate the limited ceasefire. It took effect early Tuesday and was scheduled to end Sunday evening. The period of no fighting allowed for a rare joint evacuation operation, which ended on Saturday.
About 2,000 civilians were in Oleshki
It is estimated that about 2,000 civilians were in Oleshki when the ceasefire began. Residents were given the choice of evacuating to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory or remaining in the town. The rest were provided with additional food and medical supplies.
The exact number of evacuees and those remaining in Oleshki was not disclosed for security reasons. On Saturday, relatives of the evacuees were waiting for them at the Ukrainian border, and residents of neighboring villages gathered along the road with flags and flashlights to welcome the humanitarian convoy.
“The ceasefire in Oleshki and surrounding areas of Kherson region has given residents freedom of movement, access to food, clean water and medicine, and the opportunity to regain their sense of dignity, without the constant threat of attack,“ Melania Trump said.
In parallel with the ceasefire, Moscow and Kiev have continued airstrikes in other parts of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia was attacking energy infrastructure before winter and that hundreds of thousands of families were left without electricity. According to him, Russian forces are taking advantage of the lack of air defense equipment.
Theatre in Kherson continues to work
In Kherson itself, residents have remained calm, despite expectations that the lull will end. The Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theatre “Mykola Kulish“ continues to perform in an underground room and has equipped an additional bomb shelter.
About 100 of the theatre's 120 employees continue to work in the city. Director Oleksandr Kniga said the troupe intended to continue performances next week, despite warnings from local authorities about additional Russian weapons and personnel in the area.
“Whatever happens, the performance will not be canceled,” Kniga said.
He is from Oleshki, which is on the Russian-occupied left bank of the Dnieper River. Before the war, Kniga used to commute from there to his workplace in Kherson, and now says the hope of one day returning home is among the reasons he remains in the city.
Alla Vasilenko, a theater employee, also has no intention of leaving. She cares for ten dogs and said the evacuation would require a place to live and significant funds. According to her, the trip alone would cost between 30,000 and 50,000 hryvnias.
On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater presented a concert with songs from different parts of Ukraine - from Crimea to the Carpathians. “This is also our job - to unite people and give them hope“, said Kniga.
